lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: July 1518. A woman starts dancing in a street in Strasbourg. She doesn't stop.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: She danced for days, with no music, according to the accounts. Others joined. Within a week, dozens were dancing.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: By August, estimates say between 50 and 400 people. The figure is uncertain.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Contemporary records, including a physician's notes, sermons and city council papers, do confirm the dancing.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: The council's first response was to encourage it. Guild halls were set aside, with musicians. It backfired. They then banned public dancing and music, and sent dancers to a shrine.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Deaths are often reported, up to about 15 a day. But the Strasbourg sources from the time don't mention deaths. The claims come from later accounts.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: Theories: poisoning from mouldy grain (ergot), stress-induced mass illness, religious belief. One historian rejects ergot, because poisoned people couldn't dance for days. Stress and mass illness is the most popular view.

lines.speaker: gloom
lines.text: It faded in early September. Nobody knows why it began.

scenes.caption: JULY 1518

scenes.visual: More silhouettes join in a circle
scenes.caption: 50 TO 400

scenes.caption: NOT IN THE RECORDS
